User Guide

Welcome to the Kenya ENSO Explorer

This tool helps county officers, agricultural planners, and project teams prepare for climate risks. It connects major ocean weather patterns—like El Niño and the Indian Ocean Dipole—to seasonal rainfall, farming, livestock, and flood risk across Kenya's 47 counties.

An analytical climate diagnostics platform quantifying the sub-national footprint of coupled equatorial ocean-atmosphere modes across Kenya. Synthesizes 45 years of observational gridded precipitation, remote-sensing biomass indices, and crop production data against El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), and Western North Pacific (WNP) teleconnection states across 47 IEBC county jurisdictions.

Kenya view

This view shows what the Explorer holds for Kenya as a whole: the ocean outlook, national food trade, cross-border trade and humanitarian appeals. Rainfall, harvests, pasture, floods and prices are held county by county. Switch to County to see them.

How to Use This Explorer

Analytical Workflow & Navigation

Three simple steps to explore seasonal climate risks for your county:

Three-phase diagnostic protocol for evaluating sub-national climate vulnerability:

1

Pick your county & season

1. Define Jurisdiction & Target Season

Use the dropdown bar at the top of the screen to choose your county and season (Short Rains or Long Rains). Check County context to see local population, farming numbers, and socio-economic vulnerability indicators.

Select target administrative boundary (47 IEBC counties) and boreal climatological season (OND Short Rains or MAM Long Rains). Review County context for baseline exposure metrics: agricultural and pastoral population density, cropland area, livestock holdings, and ND-GAIN vulnerability indicators.

2

Check the seasonal outlook

2. Evaluate Teleconnections & Analogues

Visit Seasonal outlook to see current ocean conditions and look at the past years that most closely resemble this season. See whether similar years brought heavier rains or drought.

Examine real-time sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies across Niño 3.4 and DMI sectors in Seasonal outlook. Inspect Euclidean analogue matches and empirical hindcast verification metrics (Tercile Probabilities, RPSS, Brier Skill Score, and False Alarm Ratios).

3

Review the historical evidence

3. Validate Observational Footprints

Explore over 40 years of rainfall records, satellite flood and vegetation maps, and county harvest data in Climate evidence. Use this evidence to back up local planning and funding proposals.

Interrogate 45 years (1981–2025) of CHIRPS precipitation anomalies, Sentinel/MODIS remote sensing (NDVI/NDWI), and MoALD crop yields in Climate evidence. Quantify statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank) to establish rigorous empirical baselines for anticipatory finance.

The Three Ocean Patterns Behind Kenya's Weather

Coupled Ocean-Atmosphere Teleconnection Mechanisms Steering Kenya's Rainfall Regimes

Kenya's seasonal rains are steered by water temperatures across three tropical oceans:

East African precipitation anomalies are dynamically coupled to equatorial sea surface temperature (SST) gradients across three primary oceanic basins:

1. El Niño & La Niña (Pacific Ocean) 1. El Niño–Southern Oscillation (Pacific Basin)

Water temperatures in the equatorial Pacific shift every few years. In Kenya, El Niño (warmer water) usually brings wetter weather and higher flood risk during the October–December short rains, especially in northern and eastern counties. La Niña (cooler water) typically brings dry spells and severe drought risk.

Modulations in central and eastern equatorial Pacific SST anomalies (Niño 3.4 region: 5°N–5°S, 170°W–120°W) alter the zonal Walker circulation. During El Niño, descending motion weakens over East Africa, enhancing low-level moisture convergence and positive precipitation anomalies during the October–December (OND) Short Rains. Conversely, La Niña enhances local subsidence, suppressing convection and driving widespread seasonal drought.

2. Indian Ocean Dipole (Indian Ocean) 2. Indian Ocean Dipole (Dipole Mode Index)

A temperature see-saw across the Indian Ocean. When the water off East Africa is warmer than normal (a Positive IOD), it pumps extra moisture inland. When a positive IOD occurs at the same time as El Niño (as in 1997 and 2023), Kenya often experiences historic, widespread flooding.

Zonal SST gradient quantified by the Dipole Mode Index (DMI: western basin 50°E–70°E, 10°S–10°N minus eastern basin 90°E–110°E, 10°S–0°). A Positive IOD (+IOD) induces anomalous low-level easterlies across the equatorial Indian Ocean, transporting massive atmospheric moisture flux directly into the Horn of Africa. Compound El Niño / +IOD events (e.g., 1997, 2019, 2023) generate extreme tail precipitation and catastrophic flooding.

3. Western Pacific Pattern (Long Rains Driver) 3. Western North Pacific Gradient & Monsoon Dynamics

During the March–May long rains, Pacific El Niño has less influence. Instead, temperature patterns across the western Pacific help steer the monsoon winds, determining whether the main rains arrive on time and how strong they will be.

During the March–May (MAM) Long Rains, standard Pacific ENSO teleconnection correlations degrade substantially due to the boreal spring predictability barrier and local convective dynamics. Intra-seasonal drivers, Western North Pacific (WNP) subtropical high dynamics, and Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) phase passages dominate seasonal onset timing and rainfall totals.

Note on regional differences: Kenya has varied climate zones. While El Niño often brings heavy rain to northern and eastern pastoral areas (like Marsabit, Wajir, and Garissa), western Kenya around Lake Victoria follows its own seasonal rainfall cycle, with significant rain from June to August. Always check your specific county rather than relying on national averages.

Sub-National Climatological Heterogeneity: Teleconnection sensitivities diverge markedly across Kenya's agro-ecological zones. Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASALs) in northern and eastern Kenya exhibit strong OND ENSO/IOD teleconnection sensitivity, whereas western highland and Lake Victoria basin regimes are governed by local mesoscale thermal circulations and tri-modal precipitation peaks (including June–August boreal summer rains). Sub-national disaggregation is therefore mandatory for valid risk assessment.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Data Sources & Administrative Framework

Geographic land area, population headcounts, and administrative ward boundaries are established under the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) 2019 Kenya Population & Housing Census (Volume I, Volume II & Volume IV) and the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) official gazette.

Boundary Universes & Sub-County Nomenclature

IEBC Electoral Constituencies vs. KNBS Administrative Sub-Counties: The 290 sub-county units mapped across this atlas represent official IEBC parliamentary constituencies (standardized as UN OCHA COD-AB Level 2 boundaries). In national statistical reporting, KNBS designates 345 administrative sub-counties. In certain counties, these universes diverge: for instance, Marsabit comprises 4 electoral constituencies (Laisamis, Moyale, North Horr, and Saku) corresponding to 7 KNBS administrative sub-counties. Both spatial definitions are administratively recognized; however, because KNBS does not publish polygon geometries for the 345 administrative sub-counties, all high-resolution spatial overlays in this explorer utilize the authoritative 290 IEBC constituency boundaries.

Population Re-Levelling & Spatial Disaggregation
  • KNBS County Level Re-Levelling: Raw unconstrained WorldPop raster sums nationally total ~55.1 million, exceeding Kenya's 2019 census population (47.56 million). All population totals in this atlas are rigorously re-levelled to official KNBS county totals (2019 Census headcount and 2026 KNBS projections).
  • Within-County Spatial Distribution: Population headcounts are distributed across constituencies using WorldPop 100 m constrained residential building footprint shares. Within each county, constituency shares are anchored to the 2020 baseline distribution, while county growth rates track official KNBS demographic projections.
  • Dominant Season Derivation & Equimodal Regimes: Seasonality classification is derived from the 30-year CHIRPS v3 (1991–2020) WMO climatological baseline. Sub-counties are classified into three distinct physical rainfall regimes:
    • Bimodal (Equimodal): Where MAM and OND seasonal accumulations differ by less than 25 mm or each season accounts for 45%–55% of the total bimodal volume (e.g. Saku in Marsabit: 289.7 mm MAM vs. 279.0 mm OND, 50.9% vs. 49.1%). In these balanced transition zones, neither season overwhelms the other, and pastoral forage replenishment depends critically on both rainfall windows.
    • MAM (Long Rains): Where MAM accounts for >55% of bimodal rainfall and exceeds OND by at least 25 mm (characteristic of western Kenya, central highlands, and Rift Valley).
    • OND (Short Rains): Where OND accounts for >55% of bimodal rainfall and exceeds MAM by at least 25 mm (characteristic of eastern pastoral lowlands including Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, and Tana River).
  • Proposal & Finance Alignment: County demographics and surface area figures align directly with the Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA) Third Basis for Revenue Sharing formula and County Integrated Development Plans (CIDPs).
Primary Dataset Citation Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (2019) 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census: Population, Households and Density by Sub-county. KNBS, Republic of Kenya.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Data Sources & Ingestion Pipeline

Official county production statistics are extracted from the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) National Agricultural Produce Reports (NAPR 2019–2024 editions), Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA) rice statistics, and the 2019 Kenya Population & Housing Census Volume IV (Distribution of Population by Socio-Economic Characteristics).

Audit Trail & Reconciliation Protocol
  • Dual-Engine Extraction: Official published report tables were extracted via dual PDF table engines (PyMuPDF and pdfplumber) with character-level coordinate verification and automated OCR cross-checks.
  • National Additivity Reconciliation: For every crop and livestock species, sub-national county values are audited against published national totals to ensure the sum of counties equals the published national figure within ±0.05% rounding tolerance.
  • Crucial Protocol: Blank ≠ Zero: An unsurveyed county or commodity in a specific reporting cycle is coded as missing (NaN / ∅ marker), NOT zero. A reported zero denotes an active survey recording zero yield. For arid rangeland counties (e.g., Marsabit, Turkana), rainfed crop farming is concentrated in isolated agro-pastoral sub-counties (e.g. Mount Marsabit / Saku); missing years reflect non-surveyed cycles rather than complete crop failure.
  • Administrative Statistics Baseline: These official statistics published by KNBS provide the recognized administrative baseline for county planning (CIDP) and project design documentation.
Primary Dataset Citation Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) (2025) National Agricultural Production Reports (2023/24, 2024/25). Republic of Kenya, Nairobi.

Participatory Valuation Architecture & Stock-Flow Decoupling

Direct downscaled econometric surfaces from global gridded models (IFPRI MapSPAM and FAO GLW4) conflated annual commercial output flow (meat offtake and milk) with standing herd capital stock, severely misrepresenting pastoralist wealth (valuing Marsabit's cattle herd at only $30.9M while omitting camels entirely). This valuation engine formally decouples:

  • Standing Capital Stock: Headcount × Standing Stock Price per head (representing living asset wealth at risk from severe multi-season droughts). For cattle, goats, and sheep, herd value is established as 75% of the market sale price based on empirical herd demographic structures (Thiakunu et al. 2024 × Kuria et al. 2016). Camels are valued using NDMA sale prices multiplied by the empirical herd structure multiplier (1.392).
  • Annual Production Flow ("Valued Commodities"): Measured as annual commercial offtake (∑ Headcount × Offtake Rate % × Sale Price) plus lactation milk yields (∑ Milking Head × Zone Milk Yield × Milk Price) plus crop harvest values plus official livestock products (eggs, honey, hides, poultry meat).
  • Full Species Scope: Reintegrates camels (283,327 head in Marsabit representing ~$108M in standing asset capital and ~$49M in annual milk and offtake flow) alongside cattle, goats, sheep, donkeys, pigs, and poultry.
  • Audited Milk Coefficients: Zone-specific lactation coefficients distinguishing arid pastoral zones (55 L/head/year), semi-arid agro-pastoral zones (100 L/head/year), and highland dairy herds (800 L/head/year) based on empirical field audits (Behnke & Muthami 2011; Field 1985).
  • Constrained Dasymetric Disaggregation: Sub-county constituency totals are apportioned from authoritative KNBS county numbers using commodity-specific spatial priors (2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census constituency livestock counts for every livestock species and product, and MapSPAM 2020 v1r2 physical crop area for crops, with constituency land-area shares where a prior is zero), strictly preserving the county sum identity (∑ Constituency ≡ KNBS County Total).
  • Data Access & Beta Governance: Prices for Kenya's 23 ASAL counties are annual medians derived from the National Drought Management Authority's County Drought Early Warning Bulletins (2019–2021). Per project data governance standards, this beta edition is provided for expert review and is not released as open-access data. No bulk download links or cloud uploads exist for these datasets.
Primary Baseline Citation Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) (2025) National Agricultural Production Reports (2023/24, 2024/25) & 2019 Census Vol. IV. Livestock pricing parameterized against NDMA Drought Early Warning Bulletins.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Official Baseline

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Climate project proposals (GCF, GEF, Adaptation Fund) frequently fail donor review because they rely on modelled or unverified third-party socio-economic indicators. We exclusively use the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics (KNBS) 2019 National Population & Housing Census and 2023 County Gender Data Sheets. These are Kenya's official national statistics used by the Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA).

Key Assumptions
  • Structural Baseline: Multi-dimensional poverty headcounts and household structures are assumed to represent decadal vulnerability baselines that exacerbate climate shock sensitivity.
  • Census Coverage: County totals are pegged directly to the official KNBS census gazetteer, with 100% additivity across all 47 counties.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Inter-Censal Drifts: Changes occurring post-2019 (e.g., population displacement following the 2020–2023 drought) are not reflected in static census tables.
  • Intra-County Heterogeneity: County-level averages mask acute disparities between urban county headquarters (e.g. Saku) and remote pastoral wards (e.g. North Horr).
Primary Dataset Citation Kenya National Bureau of Statistics; State Department for Gender; Council of Governors; UN Women (2025) County Gender Data Sheets, 2025. KNBS, Republic of Kenya.

What this sub-section is for: Shows current ocean temperatures in the Pacific and Indian oceans alongside forecasts from international climate centers (shared across all of Kenya).

What this sub-section is for: Tracks real-time planetary sea surface temperature anomalies across the equatorial Pacific (RONI/Niño 3.4) and Indian Ocean (DMI) alongside international multi-model forecast plumes (CCSR/IRI, NOAA CPC, JAMSTEC SINTEX-F).
What to do here: Inspect global ocean telemetry and ensemble plume spreads to identify planetary boundary forcing before evaluating county-specific analogue conditioning in Sub-section 2.2 before reviewing Long Rains (MAM) teleconnection diagnostics and KMD advisories.

Operational Purpose: This section equips county directors, disaster risk committees, and development partners to anchor anticipatory action in empirical physical evidence. It supports pre-season contingency budgeting, seed distribution (drought-tolerant cereals vs waterlogging-tolerant varieties), livestock disease ring-vaccination, and borehole/culvert clearing before seasonal rains commence.
The Three-Tier Early Warning Architecture:
1. Ocean Teleconnection Forcing
Global equatorial Pacific (RONI) and Indian Ocean Dipole (DMI) sea surface temperature configurations. Sets planetary boundary conditions; does not constitute a localized rainfall forecast.
2. Seasonal Rainfall Outlook
Empirical tercile probability distributions conditioned on matched historical analogues (Figure 2.1). Official seasonal forecasts and 7-day county advisories are issued by KMD.
3. Forward Impact Scenarios
End-to-end historical analogue scenarios (Figure 2.2) demonstrating how multi-hazard shocks (crop deficits, pasture crashes, floods, and market Terms of Trade deterioration) propagated during matched ocean years.

How this is county-specific: While the 8 analogue years are matched from planetary Pacific and Indian Ocean sea-surface temperatures, the rainfall history, tercile thresholds ($P_{33}, P_{67}$ in mm), and 45-year verification skill scores below are evaluated strictly from CHIRPS v3 satellite-gauge rainfall observed inside Marsabit County's boundaries. MAM Teleconnection

Long Rains (MAM) Boundary & Western-V Dynamics

Why Pacific ENSO forecasts have near-zero skill for March–May in Kenya.

A common institutional mistake is applying El Niño or La Niña forecasts to Kenya's Long Rains (MAM). In equatorial East Africa, Pacific ENSO skill drops close to zero during the boreal spring predictability barrier:

Physical Mechanisms Driving MAM Rainfall:
The Western-V SST Gradient
Differential warming between the western Pacific and Indian Ocean steers localized subsidence over Kenya (Funk et al., 2019).
Regional Air-Sea Interaction
Localized moisture convergence from the Congo Basin and southwestern Indian Ocean dominates over distant ENSO signals.
Operational Guidance
For MAM planning, county directors should consult KMD downscaled March–May outlooks rather than global ENSO news trackers.
Detailed thermodynamics in Climate Science tab
Data sources & methodology — Western-V index definition, boreal spring predictability barrier, and literature references
About this card — what it shows & how to read it
Explains why Pacific ENSO indices exhibit near-zero predictive skill during Kenya's March–May (MAM) Long Rains and summarizes the Western-V sea-surface temperature gradient mechanism (Funk et al., 2019; Liebmann et al., 2014).

Primary Sources

  • Western-V SST Gradient: Funk et al. (2018, 2019) Indo-Pacific warm pool gradient diagnostics.
  • Seasonal Predictability: Nicholson (2017) and Palmer et al. (2023) East African Long Rains teleconnection reviews.

Operational Implication

  • Zero-Skill Guardrail: Analogue tercile outlooks are always displayed alongside their leave-one-out cross-validated skill badge; when $\text{RPSS} \le 0$ (and on every MAM Long Rains outlook), a standing planning notice warns that the probabilities represent historical base-rate frequencies rather than predictive skill over 1991–2020 climatology.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this analogue method? Empirical Conditioning

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Dynamic numerical climate models often exhibit systematic rainfall biases over East Africa's complex terrain. Evaluating empirical historical analogues with matched equatorial Pacific (RONI) and Indian Ocean (DMI) sea surface temperature configurations grounds scenarios in observed physical reality.

Key Assumptions
  • Standardized Metric Space: Standardized by season-specific 1991–2020 baseline standard deviations across pre-season and concurrent windows (OND: σRONI = 0.74 lead-in / 1.12 in-season °C, σDMI = 0.37 / 0.37 °C; MAM: σRONI = 1.11 / 0.64 °C, σDMI = 0.19 / 0.22 °C) so higher Pacific variance does not dominate the Indian Ocean Dipole.
  • Live Lead-in & Plume Translation: Live lead-in coordinates use the most recently published 3-month CPC RONI season and latest single-month ERSSTv6 DMI (calculated grid supplement where CPC publication is delayed) (whereas historical candidates use JAS or DJF RONI and 3-month HadISST DMI means). Projected in-season coordinates use the IRI Niño 3.4 plume median shifted into RONI space by a fixed −0.38 °C offset alongside the JAMSTEC SINTEX-F IOD plume median.
Caveats & Limitations
  • No Two Events Are Identical: Atmospheric noise and Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) intra-seasonal pulses can modulate outcomes, and retrospective hindcast skill is an upper bound when evaluated on observed in-season ocean coordinates.
  • Operational Forecasting Guidance: Operational planning requires official seasonal forecast confirmation from the Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD).
Plain-English Statistical Guide How to Explain These Metrics to Donors & Committees
• Terciles (Rainfall Baskets): Divides 45 years into 3 equal 33% tiers (Wettest 1/3, Normal 1/3, Driest 1/3). In an unforced year, each has 33.3% equal odds. The bar shows how current ocean conditions alter these odds.
• Hit Rate (Accuracy): In 45 retrospective tests (1981–2025), how often the most favored prediction actually came true. For example, a 64% hit rate means correct in ~2 out of 3 seasons (vs 1 in 3 by chance).
• RPSS (Skill Score): Ranked Probability Skill Score tests if the forecast beats random guessing. 0.0 = coin toss; positive scores (>0.0) prove statistically significant predictive skill.
• BSS (Flood Early Warning): Brier Skill Score for the wet tercile. Measures reliability in catching dangerous flood seasons in advance to justify early action finance.
Primary Source: NOAA CPC ERSSTv6 • NOAA CPC / HadISST DMI • CHIRPS v3

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why Analogue Multi-Hazard Diagnostics? Empirical Grounding

Single-variable rainfall forecasts fail to capture compound hazard transmission. By coupling historical ocean states with satellite-derived pasture vegetative flushes (MODIS NDVI) and pastoral grain exchange rates (FEWS NET/NDMA Terms of Trade), county directors can evaluate how previous analogous seasons impacted food security, livestock markets, and emergency response budgets.

Key Assumptions
  • Standardized Predictor Space: Nearest neighbours are ranked using normalized Euclidean distance in joint RONI + DMI space.
  • Two-Season Memory: Pasture and livestock conditions depend heavily on whether the preceding MAM Long Rains were wet or dry.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Market Context: Terms of trade reflect historical commodity price regimes and macro inflation that may differ from current economic baselines.
  • Local Variations: Micro-climates and intra-seasonal dry spells can modulate local outcomes even in wet analogue years.
Primary Source: NOAA CPC ERSSTv6 • CHIRPS v3 • MODIS NDVI • NDMA / FEWS NET

Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) Official Guidance

The Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) (meteo.go.ke) is Kenya's national authority responsible for official weather forecasts, seasonal climate outlooks, and operational early warning advisories.

Platform Role & Decision Boundary: The Adaptation Atlas is a research and decision-support platform providing historical analogues and climate risk diagnostics. It does not issue operational weather forecasts or disaster directives. Operational seasonal decisions and disaster responses should always be guided by official KMD forecasts and localized advisories from County Directors of Meteorology (CDMs).

Sub-section 3.1 • Climate Graphs & Probabilities

Climate Graphs & Empirical Contingency Distributions — Marsabit

Explore over 40 years of rainfall records and drought measurements (1981–present). See how often past El Niño and positive IOD years actually brought heavy rain or drought to this county, providing hard evidence for county planning.

This sub-section provides the empirical baseline for county climate risk planning across multi-decadal satellite and ocean telemetry (1981–present)—evaluating historical precipitation, SPEI-3 drought anomalies, conditional tercile odds (Wetter vs. Drier) under coupled Pacific (ENSO) and Indian Ocean (IOD) states, and candidate driver correlations.

How to read historical records: These charts show real past weather from satellite records, not computer simulations. Keep in mind: As global temperatures warm, future rainfall patterns may intensify, and satellite estimates can sometimes miss heavy local downpours in mountainous areas.
Empirical Frequencies vs. Simulation: Observed distributions catalog historical frequencies under joint Pacific (RONI) and Indian Ocean (DMI) states rather than model simulations. Physical caveats: Multi-decadal baselines assume stationary relationships that may shift under warming, while satellite gridded precipitation can underestimate localized orographic rainfall near steep terrain.
Figure 3.1

Multi-Decadal Precipitation Climatology & Empirical Tercile Bounds

Tracks how often Marsabit experiences severe seasonal deficits or flood-producing deluge (1981–present) and how strongly those extremes align with Pacific and Indian Ocean phase shifts.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Spatial Continuity Rationale

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Ground-based meteorological stations in northern Kenya are extremely sparse—often fewer than one active, reliable rain gauge per 20,000 km². Relying purely on physical weather stations creates massive blind spots across ASAL pastoral rangelands. CHIRPS v3 (UCSB/CHC) blends cold-cloud duration satellite infrared with reporting stations to create continuous 5 km grids spanning 1981 to present. Satellite-gauge blending is the physically grounded standard to track pixel-level subcounty drought and flood anomalies continuously across Kenya.

Key Assumptions
  • WMO Climatological Baseline: Anomalies are computed against the 1991–2020 normal period (30 years) to conform to WMO standard reference rules.
  • Linear Detrending: Long-term greenhouse gas warming trends are detrended before calculating ENSO/IOD teleconnection correlations to isolate interannual ocean forcing.
  • Fixed Accumulation Windows: OND (Oct 1 – Dec 31) and MAM (Mar 1 – May 31) are treated as rigid seasonal boundaries matching agricultural calendars.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Orographic Underestimation: Thermal infrared satellite estimates systematically underestimate localized orographic rainfall around isolated mountain massifs (e.g. Mt. Marsabit, Mt. Kulal).
  • SPEI Evapotranspiration: SPEI-3 utilizes Hargreaves-Samani PET, which can over-estimate evaporative demand during hyper-thermal arid spells.
Primary Source: CHIRPS v3 (0.05°) • Vicente-Serrano SPEI-3 • s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=precipitation/source=chirps-v3/
Figure 3.1B

Consecutive Seasonal Rainfall Sequences & Compounding Drought Runs (1982–present)

Pairing Rule: Prod Year Y = OND(Y−1) + MAM(Y)

Reveals when back-to-back seasonal failures exhaust household coping capacity and prevent rangeland recovery between the Short Rains and subsequent Long Rains.

How to Read the Sequence View: Production year Y pairs the preceding Short Rains (OND of year Y−1) with the following Long Rains (MAM of year Y), matching the KNBS production-year convention where both harvests land within year Y. Each season is standardized independently against its own 1991–2020 WMO climatological baseline (never pooled). Cells are colored by standardized anomaly (z): Dry (z < −0.5, red), Normal (−0.5 ≤ z ≤ +0.5, gray), and Wet (z > +0.5, blue). Double failure years (dry / dry) are flagged distinctly as compounding multi-season drought emergencies, while the Ocean Driver State (OND → MAM) column visualizes the Pacific (ENSO / RONI), Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD / DMI), and Western North Pacific (Western-V) phases and anomalies driving each consecutive season pair.
Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Sequential Compounding Rationale

Sequences Matter More Than Averages: In East African bimodal climate regimes, single-season climate shocks can often be absorbed by household food reserves, pastoral herd condition, or regional grain trade. However, consecutive failures across both seasons trigger systemic collapse: rangeland forage deficits compound, livestock mortality accelerates, and rainfed staple harvests fail back-to-back. Averaging seasonal totals (such as OND+MAM) obscures this physical reality—a wet season and a catastrophic drought average out to "near-normal," hiding critical humanitarian risk. Evaluating the chronological sequence OND(Y−1) → MAM(Y) alongside concurrent ocean driver telemetry preserves the true multi-season shock trajectory.

Key Assumptions
  • Production Year Pairing: Year Y pairs the preceding Short Rains OND(Y−1) with Long Rains MAM(Y). Both harvests occur within calendar year Y, matching national agricultural accounting and pastoral recovery cycles.
  • Independent Seasonal Moments: OND and MAM are standardized separately against their own 1991–2020 normal period (WMO standard). The distributions have different means and variances and are never pooled.
  • Categorical Thresholds: Consistent with standard meteorological tercile definitions: Dry (z < −0.5), Wet (z > +0.5), and Near-normal (−0.5 ≤ z ≤ +0.5).
  • Unbroken Pastoral Stress Runs: Cumulative run length walks seasons in true chronological order (…OND(Y−1), MAM(Y), OND(Y), MAM(Y+1)…) counting unbroken consecutive sub-normal seasons (z < −0.5). Forage depletion compounds across seasons and does not reset at the calendar year.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Calendar Variations in 4 Counties: The production-year pairing convention (OND(Y−1) + MAM(Y)) is standard across 43 counties but knowingly differs in 4 counties where the cropping calendar is unimodal or has alternate planting regimes (project_season_year_convention).
  • Microclimatic Aggregation: County-level spatial averages blend agro-ecological zones; localized pastoral rangelands may experience multi-season drought even when high-elevation agricultural belts register near-normal rainfall.
  • Gaps vs. Zeros: Missing seasons are preserved as explicit gaps and never imputed as zero rainfall or normal conditions.
Primary Source: CHIRPS v3 (0.05°) • NOAA CPC RONI • HadISST / ERSST DMI • s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=precipitation/source=chirps-v3/
Figure 3.2

Empirical Contingency Probability Matrix (Rainfall Likelihood by Ocean Driver Strength)

Observed conditional probabilities of seasonal rainfall classes (3 Terciles at 33.3% base rate or 5 Quintiles at 20.0% base rate) conditioned on ENSO, IOD, and Western-V intensity levels (1981–present record).

How to Read Contingency Probabilities: Choose 3 (Terciles, 33%) to stratify historical seasons into equal thirds (Wetter top 33.3%, Near-normal middle 33.3%, Drier bottom 33.3%, with a 33.3% climatological base rate) or 5 (Quintiles, 20%) to stratify into equal fifths (20.0% each, with a 20.0% climatological base rate) over the 1991–2020 normal period. Use Driver Levels to switch the Y-axis between 3 standard phases and 5 intensity levels (Moderate vs. Strong), and toggle Y-Axis Ranges to display exact driver threshold bounds.
Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Non-Parametric Teleconnection Evidence

Honest Physical Limits: Standard linear correlation models oversimplify East African climate teleconnections because rainfall responses are asymmetric and non-linear. The empirical contingency matrix standardizes each seasonal ocean driver against its own 1991–2020 mean and standard deviation, stratifies the record (1981–present) into standardized z-score phase bands (3-phase: $z \ge +0.5$, $-0.5 < z < +0.5$, $z \le -0.5$; 5-level: Strong $\ge +1.5$, Moderate $+0.5$ to $+1.5$, Neutral $-0.5$ to $+0.5$, Moderate $-1.5$ to $-0.5$, Strong $\le -1.5$), and computes the empirical outcome distribution (3 Terciles at 33.3% base rate or 5 Quintiles at 20.0% base rate) for each phase. This gives planners non-parametric probabilities directly matching Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) seasonal forecasts.

Key Assumptions
  • Climatological Base Rates (33.3% vs. 20.0%): Over the 1991–2020 WMO normal period, each tercile class has an unconditional base rate of 33.3% (1/3) and each quintile class has an unconditional base rate of 20.0% (1/5).
  • Small-Sample Transparency: Phase rows with fewer than 5 historical seasons (n < 5) are flagged in amber to warn against interpreting small samples as statistical proof.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Sample Size Constraints: Super El Niño and Super +IOD events are rare extremes (n = 2–4 events in the 5-class empirical record), limiting sample sizes for extreme composite bins.
  • MAM Driver Independence: The Western-V gradient partially decouples from equatorial Pacific ENSO during the Long Rains (MAM), reflecting subtropical Western North Pacific wave trains.
Primary Source: NOAA CPC RONI • HadISST / ERSST DMI • CHIRPS v3 Terciles • s3://digital-atlas/domain=climate/type=indices/
Figure 3.3

How Strongly Do Equatorial Ocean Temperatures Govern County Rainfall?

Continuous bivariate scatter distribution, linear regression, and candidate ocean driver comparison table across the historical record (1981–present).

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Continuous Teleconnection Sensitivity

Bridging Discrete Bins to Continuous Sensitivity: While contingency matrices (Figure 3.2) group ocean drivers into coarse categorical bins, climate finance proposal writers and disaster contingency planners require exact marginal response metrics: for every +0.5°C or +1.0°C rise in equatorial Pacific SST (RONI) or Western Indian Ocean SST (DMI), how many additional millimetres or percentage points of rainfall are expected? This continuous scatter plot and ordinary least squares (OLS) regression line across all historical years (1981–2025) provides the empirical slope, Pearson correlation coefficient (r), coefficient of determination (R²), and two-tailed p-value.

Key Assumptions
  • Climatological Normal: Anomalies are computed against the WMO standard 1991–2020 reference period.
  • Linear Bivariate Modeling: OLS regression provides the linear teleconnection slope. Non-linear saturation effects during super-events (e.g. 1997, 2023) are visible as residual scatters from the trendline.
  • Seasonal Alignment: OND rainfall is paired with OND ocean indices; MAM rainfall is paired with MAM ocean indices (Western-V / WNP).
Caveats & Statistical Power
  • Collinearity: ENSO and the Indian Ocean Dipole often co-occur during OND (e.g. positive IOD + El Niño in 1997, 2006, and 2023, or standalone extreme +IOD during neutral ENSO in 2019). Raw bivariate r reflects combined ocean basin influence; check the candidate table for multi-driver variance.
  • Outlier Leverage: Extreme years like 1997 and 2023 exert leverage on the slope; points are explicitly labeled to inspect leverage.
Primary Sources: NOAA CPC RONI • HadISST / ERSST DMI • CHIRPS v3 • data/KE-enso-explorer/chirps_county.parquet

Sub-section 3.2 • Gridded Climate & Vegetation Fields

Multi-Decadal Gridded Satellite Climate & Vegetation Fields — Marsabit

High-resolution pixel-by-pixel spatial raster maps across historical seasons (CHIRPS v3 rainfall, SPEI-3 drought, MODIS NDVI vegetation condition, and FEWS WRSI crop-water satisfaction), tinted by concurrent ocean teleconnection state. Inspect historical seasons to verify spatial footprints of past droughts, wet spells, and analogue years across county wards and agricultural zones.

Why Pixel-by-Pixel Verification Matters: County-level spatial averages mask extreme local gradients across Kenya's complex topography. By inspecting per-year gridded rasters across independent earth observation systems (CHIRPS v3 rainfall, SPEI-3 drought index, MODIS NDVI vegetation health, and FEWS/USGS WRSI crop-water satisfaction), proposal teams and disaster managers can verify whether a regional teleconnection anomaly (e.g. 1997 or 2023 El Niño) penetrated into specific pastoral subcounties, grazing corridors, or highland agricultural zones.
Figure 3.4

Multi-Decadal Gridded Field History & Spatial Patterns (Per-Year Field Canvas Grid)

Maps sub-county spatial heterogeneity across historical years for Short Rains (OND)—distinguishing localized highland grazing refugia from chronically parched lowland corridors within Marsabit.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Module A: Plot Capabilities & Visual Interpretation
  • Per-Year Facet Canvas: Renders 40+ years of high-resolution gridded satellite observations in an interactive multi-column grid, clipped to official IEBC county boundaries.
  • Ocean Teleconnection Tint: Each year card is subtly tinted by the standardized anomaly (z-score) of the selected oceanic driver (PRGn diverging palette by default: green for wet teleconnection states, purple for suppressing dry states).
  • Anomaly vs. Climatology: Rainfall displays standardized departure from the WMO 1991–2020 reference normal by default (±300 mm scale), isolating true teleconnection impacts from baseline aridity.
  • Multi-Sensor Diagnostics: Switch between 4 earth observation systems to evaluate whether atmospheric moisture translated into surface drought (SPEI-3), vegetation biomass (NDVI), or crop-water satisfaction (WRSI).
Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats
  • Reference Climatology Baseline: Rainfall anomalies are computed against 1991–2020 WMO standard normal. SPEI-3 is already standard-normalized; MODIS NDVI and FEWS WRSI do not have 30-year reference baselines.
  • HTTP Range COG Streaming: GeoTIFF rasters are window-read on the fly via HTTP range requests against AWS S3 CloudFront, fetching only the county bounding box to preserve client memory.
Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary
  • Driver Independence (Frisch-Waugh-Lovell): Correlation chips display bivariate Pearson r alongside partial correlation (controlling for other drivers) to eliminate double-counting of collinear ENSO and IOD signals.
  • Multi-Driver Linear Combination: Ordinary least squares (OLS) regression calculates the optimal multi-driver variance explained (adjusted R²), identifying whether joint monitoring beats single indices.
  • Phase Intensity Gating: Categorical intensity presets filter analogue historical seasons at |z| ≥ 1.0σ (moderate) and |z| ≥ 1.5σ (strong/extreme) thresholds.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Module A: Plot Capabilities & Visual Interpretation
  • Empirical Sentinel-1 SAR Record: Tracks seasonal flood inundation across 2018–present derived from Copernicus Global Flood Monitoring (GFM) Sentinel-1 C-band synthetic aperture radar (SAR).
  • Ocean Teleconnection Phase Alignment: The ocean state strip directly below the flood time series isolates ENSO and IOD conditions for each year, highlighting severe inundation under co-occurring El Niño and positive IOD (+IOD) convergence.
  • Interactive Multi-Year OpenStreetMap Comparison: Select 1 to 4 historical years on the year strip to compare spatial inundation footprints side-by-side on zoomable OpenStreetMap panels with highway corridors and inundated settlements highlighted.
Module B: Assumptions, Limitations & Caveats
  • SAR Orbital Pass Revisit & Flash Deluges: Sentinel-1 operates on a 6- to 12-day revisit interval. Ephemeral flash floods through dry seasonal riverbeds (laggas / wadis) that drain within hours to 1–2 days may not coincide with satellite overpasses; recorded inundation thus represents an observed floor. Value 255 (unobserved orbital swaths) is strictly excluded.
  • HOT-OSM Volunteer Mapping Gaps: Health center and school counts originate from crowdsourced OpenStreetMap (HOT-OSM). In remote ASAL sub-counties, volunteer mapping coverage is incomplete. A value of zero exposed schools reflects absence of volunteer mapped points, NOT immunity to floods.
  • Endorheic Drainage Masking: Permanent open water (Lake Turkana) and seasonal salt pan depressions (Chalbi Desert) are masked using HydroLAKES and RCMRD land cover to prevent permanent lakes from being misclassified as transient flood hazards.
Module C: Methods & Analysis Summary
  • SAR Radar Backscatter Thresholding: Copernicus GFM processes Sentinel-1 SAR backscatter changes to detect standing open water, applying terrain correction and exclusion masks for steep slopes and permanent waterbodies.
  • Spatial Exposure Intersect: Performed via DuckDB spatial zonal polygon-on-raster operations, clipping flooded surfaces across official IEBC sub-county/constituency boundaries.
  • Seasonal Flood Regimes: In Kenya, OND flooding is strongly modulated by El Niño and positive IOD basin-wide surges (as in 1997, 2006, 2019, 2023), whereas MAM flooding is driven by Western-V SST gradients and convective cloudbursts flushing through dry ASAL laggas (as in 2018, 2024).

4.1 Agricultural & Livestock Production Balances — Marsabit

What this sub-section is for: Shows how past droughts and heavy rains affected crop harvests, cultivated area, livestock herds, and milk/meat output in Marsabit.
What to do here: Compare production across wet El Niño/+IOD years and dry La Niña years to identify which crops and livestock species are most sensitive to climate shocks.

What this sub-section is for: Quantifies how dual-season ocean teleconnections (preceding OND t-1 + concurrent MAM t) propagate through subnational crop yields and pastoral herd demography.
What to do here: Evaluate detrended production anomalies across ocean driver phases (Figures 4.1–4.2B) using audited KNBS NAPR and HarvestStat Africa series.

Understanding Past Impacts on Farming, Livestock, and Markets How to Navigate Historical Impacts & Vulnerability: Causal Attribution vs. Statistical Association

Section 3 established the multi-decadal meteorological patterns of rainfall and drought. Section 4 traces the consequential chain of real-world outcomes across four county-level socioeconomic and biophysical sub-sections:

4 Sector Pathways
4.1 Bimodal Crop & Livestock Balances

HarvestStat & KNBS NAPR audited series. In Kenya's bimodal system, annual agricultural output combines preceding Short Rains (OND) and concurrent Long Rains (MAM). Livestock herd mortality exhibits a 6–12 month biological lag following severe pasture droughts.

4.2 Pasture Biomass, Market Prices & Cross-Border Trade

Dekadal MODIS NDVI (2002–present) tracks continuous rangeland forage flushes and deficits. FEWS NET market prices evaluate Terms of Trade (ToT): the kilograms of maize purchased by selling 1 medium goat, alongside regional cross-border grain inflows.

4.3 Hydrodynamic Flood & Asset Exposure

Downstream exposure of populations, road networks, health facilities, schools, and electrical grids intersected with Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR observed seasonal flood inundation.

4.4 Humanitarian Emergency Chronology

UN OCHA ReliefWeb disaster situation reports (2010–present). Tracks official flash appeals, disaster declarations, and institutional relief mobilization across historical famine and deluge epochs.

Core Project Guidance — Association is Not Causation: Equatorial ocean indices alter the conditional probability distribution of seasonal rainfall, but local socioeconomic impacts are mediated by soil moisture memory, seed access, animal vaccination, road transport accessibility, and early humanitarian financing. An El Niño warming increases wet-season odds, but realized crop yields depend on agronomic management and pest dynamics.
Figure 4.1

Dual-Season Ocean Drivers vs. Agricultural & Livestock Output — Marsabit

Linking the bimodal climate signal (MAM Long Rains + OND Short Rains) to KNBS county agricultural production statistics and livestock outputs (2019–present).

The Bimodal Agricultural Attribution Reality: In Kenya's bimodal climate, annual crop production reported by KNBS is the composite result of two distinct seasonal harvests: the MAM Long Rains (planted Mar, harvested Jul/Aug, steered by the Western-V) and the OND Short Rains (planted Oct, harvested Jan/Feb of the following year, steered by IOD and ENSO). Single-season climate shocks can often be absorbed, but consecutive failures across both seasons trigger systemic collapse.
Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Official Subnational Series

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Subnational agricultural statistics in Kenya have historically been fragmented. We combine the official KNBS National Agricultural Production Reports (2019–present) with HarvestStat Africa v1.2 (1965–2024, Lee et al. 2025, Nature Scientific Data) to construct the first continuous, audited multi-decadal production series linked directly to ocean driver indices.

Key Assumptions
  • Surveyed-Period Median Index (100 = Typical): Each commodity is indexed to the median of its positive values across the surveyed years (100 × value / median, with table flags at ≥ +15% and ≤ −20%); with 3 to 6 surveyed KNBS years, no rolling window or linear detrending is applied.
  • Lagged Harvest Accounting: OND Short Rains crops are planted in October and harvested in January/February of year t+1; this physical lag is explicitly harmonized in the annual statistics.
Caveats & Limitations
  • ASAL Arid Zone Bias: In Marsabit, rainfed maize is cultivated almost exclusively on high-elevation microclimates (Mt. Marsabit and Moyale bluffs). Rangeland livestock output represents 95% of agricultural asset value.
  • Cross-Edition Discrepancies: KNBS 2023-24 vs 2024-25 editions exhibit slight rebasings (median ratio 0.96); numbers are locked to latest published KNBS revisions.
Primary Sources: KNBS NAPR (2019–present) • HarvestStat Africa v1.2 • CHIRPS v3 • MODIS MOD13Q1
Figure 4.2

Empirical Ocean Driver Phase Response vs. Mean Output — Marsabit

Empirical agricultural harvest and livestock responses (tonnes & herd counts from KNBS) conditioned on ocean teleconnection phases. While Section 2.2 quantified the meteorological rainfall hazard (mm), this figure quantifies realized economic food and livestock production outcomes.

Agronomic Output vs. Climate Hazard Why this is in Section 4, not Section 2:
Section 2.2 measures the meteorological rainfall tercile response (CHIRPS precipitation mm). Here in Section 4.2, we evaluate the realized agronomic and economic harvest response (KNBS crop production in tonnes and livestock herd counts) conditioned on the same ocean states. A wet season in Section 2.2 does not always guarantee high yield if affected by post-harvest rot or flooding, making this distinct empirical production series vital for food balance planning.
National Harvest-Aligned Attribution Convention: Production years are aligned to the seasons harvested within them: OND of the previous year (t−1) plus MAM of the reporting year (t). Short-rains drivers (ENSO, IOD) evaluate the state at OND(t−1); Long-rains drivers (Western-V) evaluate at MAM(t).
Note on Eastern Counties: In short-rains dominant counties (Tana River, Meru, Kitui, Makueni), OND of the reporting year (t) is the primary driver (r = 0.40) while MAM is negligible.
Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Empirical Phase-Conditioned Output

Conditional Harvest & Herd Response: Groups annual KNBS county agricultural production (2019–present) and HarvestStat seasonal records (1990–present) by ocean driver phase (El Niño / Neutral / La Niña via NOAA CPC RONI, or +IOD / Neutral / −IOD via DMI) to reveal the observed range, mean, and sample size ($n$) of production outcomes under each teleconnection state.

Primary Sources: KNBS NAPR (2019–present) • HarvestStat Africa v1.2 • NOAA CPC RONI / PSL DMI
Two Rulers, One Field: Figure 4.1 above (KNBS NAPR) and Figure 4.2B below (HarvestStat Africa, compiled by FEWS NET from Kenya Ministry of Agriculture archives) measure the same county with different rulers: different survey vintages, administrative district-to-county rebasings, and revision histories. Read each against its own historical baseline only — never compare an absolute value from KNBS with one from HarvestStat. That is why they are presented as separate figures.
Figure 4.2B

Multi-Decadal Seasonal Crop Harvests & Climate Teleconnections (HarvestStat Africa 1990–present) — Marsabit

Subnational seasonal crop yields, production, and cultivated area (1990–present) tied directly to planting-season rainfall terciles. Short Rains crops planted in October are anchored to year t to match OND climate drivers.

Structural Season-Year Anchoring & The Reporting Hole: In HarvestStat, every harvest is anchored to its planting year. Short Rains crops planted in October of year t and harvested in February/March of year t+1 belong to year t — aligning them directly with OND rains and El Niño / +IOD drivers. By default, the recent county era (2015–present) is displayed; the full record includes a national statistical reporting gap (2002–2014) where subnational seasonal reporting lapsed.
Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Harmonized Historical Records

The Longest Subnational Harvest Record: HarvestStat Africa v1.2 (Lee et al. 2025, Nature Scientific Data) digitizes and harmonizes subnational Ministry of Agriculture archives back to 1990. Splitting data into Long and Short Rains allows direct testing of whether wet or dry planting seasons translated into above- or below-normal harvest outcomes over three decades.

Key Assumptions
  • Era-Median Baseline (% of a Usual Year): Anomalies are computed relative to the median of each distinct administrative era (≥7 clean seasons required): 1990–2001 (district-era records remapped to 47 counties) or 2015–present (county records).
  • Quality Control Flagging: Upstream QC-flagged observations (flag > 0) are shown with dashed red outlines and excluded from medians and summary statistics.
Caveats & Limitations
  • The 2002–2014 Statistical Gap: Between 2002 and 2014, subnational seasonal crop monitoring was not systematically compiled at county level. This hatched gap represents missing records, not zero production.
  • Different Vintages from KNBS: HarvestStat and KNBS NAPR use different collection protocols and vintages. Absolute levels differ up to 2×; compare only within series.
Primary Sources: Kenya Ministry of Agriculture • FEWS NET Data Warehouse • HarvestStat Africa v1.2 • CHIRPS v3

Figure 4.3

Continuous MODIS Dekadal NDVI Pasture Biomass Dynamics (2002–present) — Marsabit

Pixel-weighted MODIS dekadal NDVI series (2002–present) across Marsabit County. Values below 100% indicate vegetative drought stress and rangeland forage deficits.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data

MODIS Terra+Aqua 250m dekadal NDVI provides continuous satellite vegetation greenness across all rangeland pastures. Evaluates whether grazing forage is in surplus (≥100% of long-term median) or drought stress (<100%), tracking vegetative recovery and crisis tipping points.

Key Assumptions

100% represents the long-term historical mean vegetation greenness for each specific dekad-of-year across county pixels. Agro-pastoral annual cycles initiate in October (OND short rains) through September (JJAS dry season), aligning with the pastoral transhumance and forage renewal cycle.

Caveats & Limitations

NDVI integrates all vegetation canopies (trees, shrubs, invasive species, and annual pasture grasses). High cloud cover during heavy rains can temporarily suppress sensor optical readings. Recent dekads are provisional until final post-processing by WFP VAM.

Figure 4.4

Pastoral Market Prices & Terms of Trade (ToT) Monthly Purchasing Power — Marsabit

Monitors retail staple food and livestock price dynamics across sentinel markets in Marsabit to detect acute collapses in pastoral household purchasing power during drought crises.

Terms of Trade (ToT) Economic Formulation & Temporal Framing: Quantifies pastoral purchasing power as the kilograms of white maize grain purchased by selling one medium live goat:
ToT (kg maize / goat) = Retail Goat Price (KES / head) ÷ Retail Maize Grain Price (KES / kg)
In normal years across Marsabit, 1 goat purchases 60–75 kg of maize grain (2008–2020 climatological baseline median: 63.0 kg/goat). During severe droughts, grazing collapses force distress livestock dumping (depressing goat prices), while grain prices soar. When ToT falls below the 25 kg/goat severe distress threshold, pastoral households experience catastrophic purchasing power collapse.
Methodological Framing Note: The severe >50% purchasing power collapse holds strictly on monthly purchasing power evaluated against trailing 24-month peaks (August 2011: −68.1% to 28.7 kg/goat; October 2022: −65.4% to 33.4 kg/goat; February 2023: −68.1% to 25.1 kg/goat across the full 2020–23 multi-season failure). Annual mean aggregation dampens these crisis troughs (2011: −32.5%; 2022: −37.6%) and masks acute seasonal distress. In addition, 2020 carries only 9 paired months in the sentinel series.
Table 4.3

Pasture Biomass Anomalies & Terms of Trade Shocks Summary — Marsabit

Historical benchmark comparison across major drought and famine crises in northern Kenya.

Causal Shock Transmission Chain Across Major Northern Kenya Droughts (2006 • 2011 • 2017 • 2020–2023)
4-Stage Physical-to-Humanitarian Cascade
1. Rainfall Failure (CHIRPS v3)
Multi-season La Niña / −IOD suppression (up to 5 consecutive failed seasons in 2020–2022).
2. Forage Collapse (MODIS NDVI)
Rangeland biomass drops to 37–58% of normal; rapid rebound to 148% during Nov 2023 El Niño flush.
3. Terms of Trade Crash (FEWS NET)
Distress livestock sales + high maize prices crash purchasing power to 25.1 kg/goat (Feb 2023; 28.7 kg in Aug 2011).
4. Food Crisis (IPC Phase 3–4)
Exchange entitlement collapse triggers IPC Phase 4 Emergency across pastoral rangelands.
• IPC Licence Compliance (CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO): Acute food insecurity phase classifications are published under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0 IGO. Phases are displayed and cited directly as contextual benchmarks and linked out; they are not blended into CC-BY-4.0 derived analytical layers.
Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Causal Transmission Mechanism

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Meteorological drought does not directly starve people; the market terms of trade do. The FEWS NET Data Warehouse (USAID) provides monthly retail and wholesale price monitoring across sentinel markets in 42 counties (2000–present). This connects oceanic temperature anomalies directly to pastoral household purchasing power and acute hunger.

Key Assumptions
  • Mandatory Detrending: Nominal Kenyan Shilling prices are deflated using national CPI and detrended to isolate climate shock spikes.
  • Terms-of-Trade (ToT) Ratio — derived, not sourced: Quantifies the purchasing power of pastoralists as the kilograms of maize grain purchased by the sale of one medium live goat. We compute it here as goat price ÷ maize price from the FEWS NET series; no agency publishes it. Being a ratio, a fall can mean either cheaper livestock or dearer grain — opposite implications for a herder — so read it alongside the two price legs above, never alone.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Sentinel Market Bias: Prices are recorded in primary subcounty hubs (Marsabit Town, Moyale, North Horr); remote nomadic camps face substantial unrecorded transport markups.
  • Cross-Border Trade Flows: Unofficial livestock inflows from southern Ethiopia during regional crises can depress local livestock prices independently of Marsabit rainfall.
  • Food Insecurity Benchmark & Licence (CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO): Official IPC acute food insecurity phases (Phases 1–5) and humanitarian caseload numbers are published by the IPC Global Support Unit and Kenya Food Security Steering Group (KFSSG). In accordance with CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO, IPC data are presented strictly for non-commercial reference and cited verbatim; they are never blended or merged into CC-BY-4.0 derived analytical layers.
Primary Sources: FEWS NET Data Warehouse retail prices • MODIS MOD13Q1 • IPC Acute Food Insecurity (CC-BY-NC-SA-3.0-IGO). Terms of Trade derived here from the FEWS price series.
Figure 4.4B

Regional Cross-Border Food Trade Flows & Market Shock Absorber (FEWS NET Cross-Border Trade [XBT])

National Border Gateways (Kenya-Wide) ℹ Why National Border Gateways?
FEWS NET Cross-Border Trade (XBT) enumerates formal and informal trade at international border posts (Namanga, Isebania, Malaba, Lwakhaka, Moyale, Taveta, Loitoktok, Lunga Lunga), not destination counties. Use the Border Post filter below to isolate a specific corridor (such as Moyale for Marsabit).

Tracking formal and informal regional grain inflows (Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia) buffering domestic market supply and capping price surges during drought years (2010–present).

The Regional Food Trade Shock Absorber: While local agro-pastoral communities experience severe harvest and pasture contractions during acute drought years, Kenya's food balance is deeply integrated into the wider East African trade basin. Surplus cereal producers in eastern Uganda (moving via Malaba and Lwakhaka) and southern Tanzania (moving via Namanga, Isebania, Taveta, Loitoktok, and Lunga Lunga) supply hundreds of thousands of tonnes of white maize grain and mixed beans, stabilizing physical market availability and preventing famine-level price spiraling. For northern ASAL counties like Marsabit, the Moyale border post serves as a vital bilateral livestock and grain exchange corridor with southern Ethiopia. In northern Kenya, the Moyale border post serves as a vital bilateral livestock and grain exchange corridor with southern Ethiopia. For annual national food balances, import dependency ratios, and global customs origins across ten commodities, see Food Trade →
Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Regional Trade Buffer

The "Whole-of-System" Trade Reality: Drought does not respect administrative borders, but neither do regional food markets. The FEWS NET East Africa Cross-Border Trade (XBT) monitoring system tracks formal and informal commodity movements across 34 border crossing points throughout the Greater Horn of Africa (2010–present). Measuring these trade flows reveals how regional spatial variability in rainfall buffers national food availability when Kenya experiences widespread Long or Short Rains failures.

Key Assumptions
  • Informal Trade Enumeration: In addition to customs declarations, trained FEWS NET border monitors observe informal cross-border movements (head loads, bicycles, handcarts, unmonitored trucks) to capture unrecorded trade.
  • Bilateral Kenya-Touching Flows: Includes all registered commodity flows where Kenya is the destination (Import) or country of origin (Export). Transit trade through Kenya to third countries is excluded.
Caveats & Limitations
  • National Resolution: XBT records transactions at national border points (Namanga, Isebania, Malaba, Lwakhaka, Moyale, Taveta, Loitoktok, Lunga Lunga), not destination county markets. Flows represent national market buffer capacity.
  • Price & Policy Distortions: Trade volumes are shaped by export bans, regional import tariffs, currency fluctuations, and nontariff trade barriers as well as agro-climatic deficits.
Primary Source: FEWS NET East Africa Cross-Border Trade (XBT) Monitoring • FAO GAUL 2024 • IEBC COD-AB Boundaries

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Operational Radar Physics

The "Best Available Data" Reality: Optical satellite sensors are completely blinded by heavy convective storm clouds during flood crises. Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR is the sole operational sensor emitting microwave radar pulses to penetrate cloud cover and map open water at ~111 m. Intersecting with official KNBS Census counts and projections distributed by WorldPop 100m building footprint shares provides the ground-truth count of exposed populations.

Key Assumptions
  • Census-Anchored Spatial Distribution: Population totals are calibrated to official KNBS census levels (and annual projections for post-2020 events), distributed proportionally across constituencies using WorldPop 100 m building footprints.
  • Year-Matched Denominators: Observed flood events are matched against the population denominator of their respective flood year (multi-year sums mix population vintages).
  • Maximum Seasonal Footprint: Observed extents represent the seasonal composite union of all inundation detected across Sentinel-1 orbital passes.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Orbital Revisit Gaps (Blank ≠ Zero): Sentinel-1 revisit interval is 6–12 days; flash floods cresting and draining within 24h between passes are not recorded.
  • Radar Mask Value 255: Denotes unobserved radar shadow or permanent water—never dry land.
Primary Source: Copernicus GFM Sentinel-1 SAR • KNBS Census Level & Projections (WorldPop 100m share) • s3://digital-atlas/domain=exposure/type=intersect/region=kenya/processing=analysis-ready/

Official Humanitarian Situation Reports & Appeals — Marsabit — All Kenya

Click report titles to inspect the original full documentation, damage assessments, and humanitarian response bulletins on ReliefWeb.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Humanitarian Ground-Truthing

Ground-Truthing Climate Anomalies: Meteorological indices and satellite NDVI monitor physical environmental departures, but UN OCHA ReliefWeb situation reports capture the humanitarian institutional response—documenting when local coping capacities broke down, official government disaster declarations were issued, and international appeals were launched.

Key Tagging Rules
  • First-Match Classification Hierarchy: Reports tagged with multiple simultaneous hazards are classified deterministically in order of priority: Drought → Flood → Epidemic → Other. For example, compound drought and flood reports are counted under Drought.
  • County Matching: Reports are matched to the selected county based on normalized administrative tags, ensuring zero empty counties.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Reporting Attention vs. Hazard Severity: Report volume measures reporting volume, donor visibility, and agency footprint—not physical severity alone. High report counts reflect active emergency appeals and media cycles.
  • Snapshot Vintage: The dataset represents a verified snapshot harvested via the ReliefWeb API spanning January 2010 through June 2026.
Primary Sources: UN OCHA ReliefWeb (reliefweb.int API, 15,736 county-tagged reports across all 47 counties).

Figure 4.7

Production, Imports and Exports by Commodity

How domestic production compares with recorded trade, and how much apparent supply came from imports.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? National Supply Balance

Physical Production vs. Recorded Trade (1990–2024): Comparing domestic harvest volumes against international imports and exports on a shared physical tonnes scale reveals whether Kenya relies on external markets to meet staple demand or exports most of its output.

Key Definitions & Timing Rules
  • Production definition: FAOSTAT production item 56, Maize (corn): matches the trade item.
  • Maize harvest index & response windows: In the maize Harvest and imports view, harvest index equals 100 × production(Y) / median(5 previous reported years). Years below 90 are shortfalls; consecutive shortfall years form an episode with a shaded response window spanning the episode through the following calendar year (end + 1). Years without five prior reported harvests show no baseline.
  • Ocean-to-harvest alignment (Timing rule 1): Harvest year Y is read against the short rains of the year before, OND(Y−1), and the long rains of the same year, MAM(Y), because Kenya's short rains run October–December before the calendar year and the long rains run March–May inside it.
  • Trade reporting & no single lag (Timing rule 2): Trade is reported January to December, so imports answering a poor harvest arrive partly in the same calendar year and partly in the next (and as FAOSTAT notes, a crop harvested at the end of a calendar year is used mostly in the following year). This view therefore assumes no single lag.
  • Observed peak timing (Timing rule 3): Computed dynamically from the selected maize record (for 1990–2024: following year after 1993 and 1996, within the episode during 2008–2009, and in the shortfall year itself in 2017 and 2022). For multi-year episodes where the peak falls inside the episode itself, it is described as “within the episode”.
  • Source flags: FAOSTAT marks each value as official (A), estimated (E), imputed (I) or from an international organisation (X). The data table shows the flag for every year.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Calendar-year allocation (FAOSTAT QCL): Per the FAOSTAT Crops and Livestock Products methodology, production is allocated to the calendar year in which the entire harvest or the bulk of it took place.
  • Stocks excluded & timing vs. cause: Apparent balance is production plus imports minus exports without carry-over stock adjustments. Imports also move with prices, policy and stocks; the harvest-and-imports view shows timing, not cause.
  • Food Balance Sheets not mixed: FAOSTAT Food Balance Sheets cover broader product groups and treat stocks differently, so they are not mixed into this physical commodity series.
Primary Sources: FAOSTAT Crops and Livestock Products (QCL & TCL, 1990–2024) • UN Comtrade (HS 060311 cut roses).
Figure 4.8 & Table 4.6

Where Recorded Trade Came From and Went To

Reported trading partners for one commodity and flow, and how their shares changed between years.

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Bilateral Partner Concentration

Identifying Supply Origins & Export Markets (2010–2025): Bilateral customs declarations show whether Kenya's staple food imports are concentrated in a single regional neighbour or diversified across global suppliers, and how partner shares shift across years.

Key Definitions
  • Product definitions: Maize excludes seed. Wheat excludes durum; lines reported under HS 2007 or earlier include seed. Rice is milled and broken. Sugar covers selected raw and refined lines. Beans cover selected species. Tea is black tea, coffee is green coffee, flowers are roses only.
  • Partner share basis: Each partner's share is its reported customs value divided by the reported World total for that commodity, flow, and year.
Caveats & Limitations
  • Unreported years: Kenya submitted no annual Comtrade reports for 2011, 2012, and 2014. Those years are left blank, never imputed as zero.
  • Partner country only: Customs records identify the partner country of origin or destination; they do not record transport mode or port of entry.
Primary Sources: UN Comtrade Bilateral Customs Declarations (2010–2025, nominal US$).

Selected Export Earnings and Staple Import Bill

Data Sources & Planning GuidanceData Provenance, Methodology & Limitations
Why this data & analysis? Macroeconomic Trade Balance

Comparing Agricultural Export Earnings Against Staple Food Imports (2013, 2015–2024): Placing Kenya's four flagship agricultural exports (tea, coffee, cut roses, avocados) alongside the five major food imports (maize, wheat, rice, refined sugar, palm oil; plus optional dry beans) illustrates their relative scale in nominal US dollars.

Completeness Rules
  • Component sources: FAOSTAT trade values are used for every component except cut roses, which use UN Comtrade reported World totals.
  • Strict completeness gate: A basket total and ratio are computed only in years where every component in both baskets is observed (2013, 2015–2024).
Caveats & Limitations
  • Not a financing identity: Showing export earnings beside the staple import bill does not imply that export revenues directly pay for food imports, nor does it measure foreign-exchange reserves or household welfare.
  • Fixed four-crop scope: The export basket is restricted to the four specified product lines (tea, green coffee, cut roses, and avocados) so each series has a single, non-overlapping product code.
Primary Sources: FAOSTAT Trade Crops & Livestock (TCL) • UN Comtrade (HS 060311 cut roses).
